name: entity
intent: Give a domain concept a stable identity that survives attribute changes, representation changes and time, and define its equality, lifecycle and lookup in terms of that identity instead of in terms of its attributes.
problem: A model that compares objects by their attributes cannot answer whether two instances are the same thing: a customer whose e-mail and plan changed looks like a different customer, while two distinct people who share a name look like one. References held by other objects, caches and audit records break silently, and every state change forces callers to re-identify the object.
context: Rich domain models in which some concepts must be tracked through time: the object is created, changes state, is stored and reloaded, and may exist in several representations (in-memory instance, database row, message payload, UI snapshot) that all have to denote the same thing. It is the modelling decision that pairs with Value Object: attribute clusters become values, while the things whose history matters keep an identity.
benefits: Identity survives change: a customer who changes name, address or plan is still the same customer, so long-lived references, audit trails and business continuity keep working.
Equality, hashing and collection membership get one stable definition - the identity - which removes the silent bugs of attribute equality, such as a set entry disappearing after a field changes.
Identity-based lookup becomes possible: repositories, caches and identity maps can return exactly one in-memory object per logical entity, so two copies of the same row cannot diverge unnoticed.

The mutable part of the model becomes safe to use: the entity may change state through domain methods while callers keep valid references, because a reference denotes the identity, not a snapshot of the attributes.
Identity can be typed: a dedicated identity value object (CustomerId, OrderId) keeps identifiers of different concepts from being mixed up, in the languages that can check it at compile time.

The store can stay out of the model: because identity is the contract between the object and its storage, mapping, caching and reloading live in a repository or data mapper instead of leaking into domain behaviour.
tradeoffs: Mutable shared state: an entity is deliberately mutable, so aliasing bugs, stale in-memory copies and data races appear as soon as two callers hold the same object; continuity is bought with mutation discipline.

Identity must be assigned once and never reassigned, but generated surrogate keys are usually unknown until insert; deriving equality or a hash code from a not-yet-assigned key corrupts hash-based collections (the classic JPA/EF Core failure).

Equality has to be written and maintained: equals/hashCode (or the language equivalent) must agree with identity and with the framework's proxies and lazy loading, and the ORM may fight it (proxies not equal to their target, data classes hashing every field).

Modelling too much as entities produces a mutable object graph with lifecycle and persistence overhead where an immutable value object would have sufficed; entity parts are slower to load (separate tables, joins) and harder to test than values stored with the root.
Reference navigation invites lazy loading and N+1 access patterns: loading by identity is cheap, but following entity-to-entity associations is where object-relational impedance is felt.
A globally unique identity is a handle: any component that holds the identifier can resolve the entity, so authorization and tenant isolation must be enforced outside the entity itself.

participants.responsibility: The domain object whose equality, continuity and lifecycle are defined by identity; its attributes change over time while it remains the same conceptual thing.
An immutable identifier (preferably a typed value object) assigned once at creation and never changed; the sole basis for equality, hashing and lookup.
Obtains or generates a fresh identity for new entities and passes the existing identity back when reconstituting an entity from storage or a message.
Resolves an identity back to the entity and, together with an identity map or unit of work, guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session.
Code that holds, passes and compares entities by identity instead of comparing their attributes, and treats detached copies as snapshots rather than as entities.

use_cases: Master data tracked for years — customers, accounts, contracts, products, patients — where attributes change but the business entity stays the same (e.g., a Customer who moves house is still the same Customer).
Documents with a lifecycle: orders, invoices, bookings and shipments that move through states (pending → paid → shipped → delivered) while remaining the same document with a stable order number.

Shopping cart to order transition: a ShoppingCart is reconstituted as an Order with the same customer identity but a new order identity, preserving the correlation to the customer while starting a new business process.

Correlating representations across layers: an entity persisted as database rows, published as domain events, and displayed in a UI must be recognisable as the same thing in all three — identity is the correlation key across representations.
In-memory session consistency: a unit of work or identity map ensures the same Customer loaded twice in one request is one object reference, preventing edits from silently diverging into two copies.
Referencing across bounded contexts: one microservice holds a CustomerId reference to another service's aggregate root, allowing independent deployment and loading without a direct object pointer.

Healthcare records: a Patient entity persists across multiple visits, lab results and prescriptions — the patient identity is the anchor for the entire medical history regardless of demographic changes.
Versioned documents: an InsurancePolicy entity may be replaced by a new version while the original policy number (identity) remains the correlation handle for auditors and legacy systems.

Hibernate/JPA: an @Entity class with an @Id is managed by the persistence context, which guarantees one in-memory instance per identity per session — loading the same row twice in a session returns the same object reference, an Identity Map built into the framework.

Entity Framework Core: identity resolution makes the DbContext track a single entity instance per primary key, so duplicate instances arriving in a deserialized graph are merged into the already-tracked entity instead of diverging into two tracked copies.

Drupal Entity API: nodes, users and taxonomy terms (content entities) and roles or image styles (configuration entities) are identity-bearing objects with typed storage handlers, revisions and field bundles behind one CRUD and validation API.
avoid_when: The concept is completely defined by its attribute values and its instances are interchangeable: model it as a Value Object - immutable, with equality by attributes.
The object is a transport or read model (DTO, request/response payload, projection row): those have no lifecycle of their own, so a record or struct without identity semantics is simpler.
The concept is an operation or a stateless computation: model it as a domain service or a function instead of inventing an id for it.
The data is append-only event history or a query result set that is never updated: identity adds nothing beyond the key the data already carries.
anti_patterns: Attribute-based equality on an entity: two instances of the same customer compare unequal as soon as one field changes, and the customer fetched twice becomes two customers.
Mutable identity: the id is reassigned after insert or fixed up on merge, which silently changes what the object denotes and corrupts caches, sets and audit trails.
Entity as table row: getters and setters mirror the schema, behaviour lives in services alongside it, and the entity degenerates into a persisted DTO with an id.

Rebuilding the framework's identity machinery on top of an ORM - a hand-rolled map keyed by id next to the change tracker - or storing entity copies as serialized values so the same logical entity exists in several divergent instances.
design_principles: Encapsulation: identity is immutable and state changes only through intention-revealing domain methods, so the entity guards its own invariants.
Single responsibility: identity assignment and lifecycle management belong to a factory or repository, not to the entity's business methods.
Substitutability: equality and hashing must form a consistent equivalence relation (same identity implies equal and equally hashed) for collections and caches to behave.
Favour composition over inheritance: build entities from value objects instead of attribute fields, and reference other entities by identity instead of by pointer.
Persistence ignorance (dependency inversion): the model must not depend on the mapping infrastructure, which is why the identity - not the table - is the contract.
best_practices: Assign identity once — generated by a factory or repository for new entities, or passed in when reconstituting from storage — and make the identity field readonly/immutable for the entity's lifetime.

Prefer a typed, branded identity value object (CustomerId, OrderId) over a raw int or string: this prevents cross-type mixups (a UserId accidentally used where an OrderId is expected) in languages with static type checking.

Define equality and hashing on identity alone. In runtimes that guarantee one instance per identity (e.g., ORM change-tracked sessions), document that reference equality suffices; otherwise override equals/hashCode (or the language equivalent) to compare only the identity field.

Expose state changes through intention-revealing domain methods (e.g., Order.addItem(), Order.confirm()) rather than public setters, so the entity can enforce invariants and emit domain events on significant transitions.

Model state transitions as explicit guarded transitions — treat the entity as a state machine where invariants (e.g., an Order cannot ship before being confirmed) are enforced in the transition method, not in external services.
Keep entity aggregates small: reference other aggregate roots by typed identity (CustomerId) rather than by object-graph navigation, to preserve consistency boundaries and avoid deep耦合.
Maintain one in-memory instance per identity per unit of work: use an identity map to prevent two copies of the same entity from diverging; treat detached or serialized copies as read-only snapshots.
Use a base entity class or mixin to centralise identity storage, equality-by-identity, and hashing, so concrete entities only override behaviour and invariants.
Never expose the identity as a public writable setter after construction: identity mutation corrupts identity maps, hash-based collections, caches and audit trails.
Emit domain events (OrderSubmitted, PaymentAuthorized) from entity methods on significant state transitions to keep external components decoupled from the entity's internal mutation.
Keep entity creation behind factory methods or constructors that enforce constructor-level invariants, ensuring a partially-constructed entity can never reach a repository or client code.
Audit entity lifecycle: track who created an entity and when, and record significant state transitions with timestamps and actor identity, either via domain events or a separate audit log.

When using an ORM, configure equality/hashing at the application level (entity base class) rather than relying on the ORM's generated proxies, to avoid the common bug where a proxy is not equal to its target entity.
